preamble: Loss of the velar nasal /ŋ/ is documented across unrelated language families, most often in word-initial position, where /ŋ/ is cross-linguistically rare. It is an ongoing change in Hong Kong Cantonese, where onset /ŋ/ is merging with the zero onset, and a completed one in Mandarin, which lost the Middle Chinese ŋ- initial (我 MC ngaX > wǒ). Initial-consonant loss is also a hallmark of several Pama-Nyungan subgroups in Australia, including Northern Paman (Uradhi ani < *nga:ni 'what') and Arandic (Arrernte aye- < *ngayu 'I'); Arabana dropped /ŋ/- within the historical record, and Nanai lost Proto-Tungusic initial *ŋ- (*ŋindakun > инда 'dog'). In Finnic the loss is word-internal: *ŋ disappeared except before k, with compensatory lengthening (*jäŋe > jää 'ice').

examples.note: Onset /ŋ/ is lost in light-tone syllables in younger speakers' speech, merging with the zero onset; prescriptivists stigmatize it as 'lazy pronunciation' (懶音).
The velar nasal initial of Middle Chinese is lost in Mandarin; Cantonese 我 ngo5 keeps it.
Compensatory lengthening; *ŋ was lost except before k.
Initial *ŋ is lost in Northern Paman; Mpalitjanh, Yinwum, Linngithigh and Ngkoth also have ani. Kuuk Thaayorre nga:n keeps it.
Arandic lost initial consonants; Nhanda ngayi and Kalkatungu ngayi keep the nasal.
Kaytetye erlwe 'forehead' shows the same loss.
Initial /ŋ/ elision in Arabana continued into the 20th century.
Ulch ӈэнэву (ŋēnewu), Evenki ӈэнэдемӣ keep ŋ.
Orok ӈинда keeps ŋ; Manchu indahūn also lacks it.
Ulch has ӈуй alongside уй; Nanai keeps ŋ in ӈа̄ла 'hand' (*ŋāla).
